en: While still too young to grow,
Let us put him to death.
Let us crush his belly beneath our feet,
And renounce all kinship
With this wretched boy.
Let us pour sand into his mouth;
If our hands cannot kill the child,
Let us destroy him utterly,
Make all his days dark,
And find some way to do it.
Then the affairs of the age will prosper,
And such crookedness will vanish.”
Saying these words then,
I sharpened my black tongue
And spoke out before the khan.
“She is only a woman,” they said,
“From time immemorial,
A woman’s deeds have been flawed,” they said,
And hobbled my thoughts short.
“They have become enemies,” they said.
Why should my wretched, dishonored mother
Regard as an enemy
A child still in the womb?
I have no steed but my gray horse,
And apart from Külchoro and Kanchoro,
I have no other kin.
When I stoop, I have no saddle,
And to accompany and support me,
I have no nephew born of an elder sister.
I have no elder brother to uphold me,
No maternal uncle to lean upon,
No younger brother to be my companion.
While Külchoro and Kanchoro,
Those two with rhyming names, remain,
I have no brothers but those two,
And without them I have no life.
What lives today is gone tomorrow;
My heart is aflame, my breast is embers,
All for the two boys with matching names.
“Just see how he lies,” she said,
And because of Kanchoro
She utterly shamed her.
Before all the people, his mother,
The foal of a surging river,
Was left whining like a howling dog.
Venom scattered across my face,
My mouth was sealed and could not open,
My honor scattered like ashes.
My heart burned and became embers,
My mouth faltered before speaking,
Then opened without the slightest movement,
And the fierce words leaving my mouth
Scattered like fire across the earth.
Koshoy and Bakai were there,
Men who had worn out horses and seen many lands,
With heroes of countless kinds,
And all the Kyrgyz people.
My soft-fledged pale falcon,
My morning star born of my own flesh.
You mangled my words,
And brought shame upon me;
You scattered my speech abroad,
And made me a public disgrace.
My wounded pride struck the earth;
The mouth that spoke was stopped.
I, the wretched, dishonored woman,
Breathed only through my back;
Through toil I won my people.
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
I sent out to serve me.
I prepared a white, gleaming sword.
I raised an Argyn and made him a man.
While Kanchoro was still a child,
I thought of slaughtering him.
When the trembling sun was setting,
When the people’s herds had settled,
And the folk lay down in peace,
My thoughts departed, wretched as I was.
I opened the hearth and faced the heights—
Who is there to hear these words of yours?
Let the dark and gloomy night hear;
Who else but it can hear?
Your words are not fitting;
Mother, your words came like an enemy’s.
Clear your clouded brow,
And, suffering mother who raised me,
Close your mouth and nose.
Oh, this will bring you shame;
Remain where you are,
For what you contemplate is monstrous.
This deed will bring disgrace;
Stay among those distant people.
My chosen Külchoro,
The banner borne by my spear,
Companion of my khanly father,
The gift of Khan Almambet,
The remnant of my beloved,
The lock upon all I built,
The heart of the marketplace.
These boys are Bagdagül’s morning stars,
The support of my fleshly heart,
The mates of those I have left,
The finest of the beloved ones.
My father’s lion,
The Kyrgyz people’s eagle,
The Chubak of Khan Baltai.
On the rugged forked mountain pass,
With my father, the lion Manas,
He swore friendship for the next world;
He is the beloved of this entrusted soul.
The flower-filled hope of my heart,
The son of my foster-father Chubak—
This Kanchoro is that son.
See how this ill-fated mother of mine
Understands none of this!
She says the infant in the womb
Sucked her breast till she wailed,
And so became her mortal enemy—
My mother, darkened by misfortune.
When he was still an infant,
She had the spirits carefully guard him,
And had costly crimson cloth
Laid over him in splendor.
She appointed sixty blood-shedding champions
To shed blood in his defense,
To rout whoever attacked,
And destroy whoever caused loss.
She set young women to guard him,
And slaughtered barren mares and young camels
To provide for his nourishment.
She had Margalan and Kokon searched,
And red raisins and sweet foods
Brought from every city.
Tender lamb and savory head-meat
She had simmered into broth.
Until you reached the age of seven,
She had the young women taste your food
And carefully prepare each meal,
Making every limb of yours whole,
Leading you with her until you became a man.
Across countless roads of no return,
She had the routes reconnoitered,
And horses brought from afar.
She had you thrust spears at the enemy,
Drag your spear through their ranks,
And learn the enemy’s ways.
She made your spirit mighty
And made you sultan and khan of the Argyn.
While your mighty uncle lived,
You became a man of weighty renown;
You kept a royal court and became khan.
You became a worthy hero,
Sound in all your twelve limbs.
While you had such an uncle,
When did you ever lack anything?
Ruling the people and maintaining the realm,
You became a seasoned lion.
As for the remaining Kanchoro,
You anointed yourself with bloody fat,
To remove the wretch
From this world forever.
“Do not let him stir up strife through the ages;
Finish him and be done with it.
Champion of the holy old man,
My comrade, lion Bakai,
Make the child disappear,
And turn him into black earth.
Jamgyrchy of the Eshetek,
Kutunu, the very eldest,
And round-eyed Sarkangan,”—
When the stars shone bright,
At the hour when the people slept,
They took these men as envoys
And called upon the people to mediate.
“This child is my darling,” they said,
And pulled him from my hands.
When God was about to punish
My crazed, unruly mother’s intent,
The wretch’s purpose went astray.
Fearing she would harm the child,
They saved him from brutal torment
And pulled him from my hands.
They did not rightly heed my words,
But regarded me as an enemy
And had him taken from my hands.
They had him securely confined in a palace
Where not even a crow could fly,
Whose walls were guarded by lions,
And which even spirits could not cross.
From a city of Hindustan,
The mother of seventy sons,
The sovereign among women,
The noble matron Adalsur—
They summoned Adalsur.
They hung an amulet around his neck,
And entrusted him to Adalsur,
The holy old man’s Adalsur.
She set his crooked affairs right
And raised him with tender indulgence.
My whole body turned to blood,
And both my arms were palsied.
This wretched one, unable to drink kumiss,
Longed even for muddy water.
A sorrowful day arose and became my fate;
My mouth, which could not hold a grain of wheat,
Swelled to the size of a bull’s head.
My mouth, which could not hold a grain of millet,
Swelled to the size of a heifer’s head.
My strength waned as the days passed,
And I endured a dog’s humiliation.
I wished to die, but could not;
I sobbed, unable to give up my soul.
Suffering was heaped upon suffering,
And yesterday the tears from both my eyes
Streamed down over my breast.
The wide world became narrow;
This once-magnificent soul
Longed even for muddy water.
My valiant son was lost,
And Külchoro departed in grief,
His two hands bound,
His neck pierced through,
His back slashed by the foe.
My Chürök wept and beat herself;
Her fair breasts, round as apples,
Were split open by the lash.
They rode wretched mares, jolting along,
And hung loosely in their felt cloaks
When they were carried off as booty.
Our villages stood side by side;
Our birth cords were cut and our swaddling washed together—
From our roots onward, we were inseparable.
When we rode against the foe, our cries were one;
When we went to battle, our banner was one;
When we fought, our dust was one;
Our souls were close, our lives were one.
I told you to heed my words;
I told you to cast your eyes upon us.
The treasure left as a legacy,
Your bloodthirsty uncle and lion,
You joined with Er Kyyaz to destroy.
You burned and cast aside Keng-Kol,
And set a grievous fire among your kin.
You took Chachykey as booty,
And took the mourning widow for a wife.
You broke open the treasury and took the money;
You divided the Kyrgyz and took slaves.
You seized the mountain passes, spreading terror,
And laid waste to the people.
My son, you stained your spear with blood;
You destroyed your own uncle
And fastened this deed securely.
You burned my plane tree and raised an uproar;
You bound my sapling in black.
You exhausted my treasury and possessions
And brought all my laughter to an end.
